narrative.text: Explains that the guidance highlights how immunization, sexual and reproductive health and cancer control programmes can prepare for national HPV vaccine introduction under the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy.

Describes cervical cancer as the second most common cancer in women worldwide, with about 500 000 cases and 250 000 deaths a year, mostly in low-income countries, and nearly all linked to HPV infection, especially types 16 and 18. It explains that HPV infection usually clears but can persist and lead to precancerous lesions over decades, which screening can detect, and that visual inspection with acetic acid and cryotherapy offer a simpler approach for low-resource settings. It also notes the 2005 World Health Assembly resolution on cancer prevention and control and early vaccine trial results showing near-complete protection.

Explains that HPV vaccines are made of non-infectious virus-like particles and that two prophylactic vaccines have shown excellent efficacy against precancerous lesions linked to the vaccine types, with the quadrivalent vaccine also preventing genital warts. It notes the vaccines are expected to prevent about 70% of cervical cancers in HPV-naive women and that questions on long-term efficacy, boosters and special populations are still being studied.

Argues that HPV vaccines should be given before sexual debut and notes they will likely be licensed for girls and women aged 9–26, with stronger immune responses in young adolescents and possible catch-up vaccination. It describes the expected availability of Cervarix and Gardasil and the uncertain benefit of vaccinating males, younger children, people with HIV and pregnant women. It links vaccine introduction to WHO's reproductive health strategy and its call to use existing services as entry points.
Notes that HPV vaccines could strengthen links between health services and prevent a common cancer as well as genital dysplasia and warts on a large scale, and introduces their key features.

Explains that HPV vaccines need new delivery approaches because they target adolescents rather than infants, involve many stakeholders and bring immunization programmes into the sensitive area of sexual health. It describes the Global Immunization Vision and Strategy's aim to extend immunization to other age groups and the hard priority choices cancer programmes face. It sees the vaccines as a chance to promote delayed sexual debut and condom use, which will depend on strong partnerships between programmes.

Notes that HPV vaccines are likely to cost much more than traditional EPI vaccines and that international financing, for example through GAVI, is being discussed. It warns that cost should not be the only criterion and that private-sector introduction among affluent groups could widen health inequities.

Stresses that HPV vaccine delivery must be affordable, feasible and culturally acceptable and that backlash against sexual and reproductive health programmes must be avoided. It calls for clear complementary messages on delaying sex, condom use, HIV prevention and screening, and hopes the vaccine will spur cervical screening where it is lacking.

Argues that programmes must find new ways of working together and with the private sector, and that international partnerships are needed to shorten delays in vaccine access for developing countries. It highlights the challenge of balanced communication about the vaccines' benefits and limits and of presenting them within a wider strategy to prevent cervical cancer deaths.

Sets out key messages for presenting HPV vaccines, such as HPV causing over 99% of cervical cancers, being very common and highly transmissible, and often having no symptoms. It notes the vaccines' high efficacy in HPV-naive young women and stresses explaining clearly what they can and cannot do, alongside lifestyle information for young people.

Lists action points on advocacy, information and communication, such as gathering country data on cancer burden and HPV strains, tailoring communication strategies to stakeholders, decision-makers and communities, and basing health promotion on local needs. It also covers developing materials and training for health workers and addressing financing questions such as insurance coverage. It urges using HPV vaccination to strengthen existing programmes for adolescents, such as school-based education on sexual health, nutrition, tobacco and HIV.

Explains that the likely licensed age range of 9–26 years should be split into a primary target group, probably girls aged 9–13, and a catch-up group. It discusses reaching young girls through school-based programmes, where attendance is high, or through EPI or tetanus vaccination campaigns.

Describes ways to reach adolescents who are not in school, such as community-based sexual and reproductive health programmes or vouchers, while noting their limited delivery experience and cold-chain constraints. It discusses the catch-up group of women aged 14–26, warning against diverting resources from the primary cohort, and suggests using screening, STI and HIV services to spread messages. It stresses that vaccinated women still need screening and that vaccines should be delivered within comprehensive, rights-based services rather than stand-alone programmes.

Recommends building HPV vaccine delivery on existing structures such as the cold chain, with the immunization programme likely leading in partnership with sexual and reproductive health, adolescent health, cancer control and HIV programmes. It also calls for links with education services, civil society and the private sector.

Advises planning early for monitoring and evaluation, using routine immunization surveillance for process indicators and tracking earlier outcomes such as genital warts and precancerous lesions. It also calls for adverse event monitoring that captures HIV status and pregnancy, use of cancer registries or proxies, and private-sector cooperation on reporting.

Lists action points for national programmes on service delivery, such as linking stakeholders, defining the primary target group, addressing sociocultural barriers, checking school attendance and updating cervical cancer strategies. It also calls for comprehensive cervical cancer prevention including screening, treatment, vaccination and monitoring of effectiveness.

Stresses that strengthening health systems and financing HPV vaccine purchase must be high priorities, with some decisions taken at global or higher government levels. It discusses the need for epidemiological data, demand forecasting and lessons from hepatitis B vaccine introduction, and the importance of international funding through GAVI, UNICEF and the PAHO Revolving Fund to expand supply and secure lower prices. It also covers government oversight of private-sector introduction, such as reporting of adverse events and post-marketing surveillance.

Lists stewardship and financing actions, including setting up a national HPV vaccine working group, developing demand and financing models and a business case for public and private funding. It stresses integrated delivery, partnerships, closing knowledge gaps and developing detailed delivery guidelines.

Concludes that the HPV vaccine is one element of comprehensive cervical cancer control and warns that, without attention to poorer women, it could widen health inequities. A note added in proof reports the US FDA's June 2006 approval of the quadrivalent vaccine Gardasil for girls and women aged 9–26 and lists the conditions it is intended to prevent.
Lists web links to UNFPA, WHO, GIVS and GAVI as additional resources.

The front matter of WHO's 2006 guidance 'Preparing for the introduction of HPV vaccines: policy and programme guidance for countries', with copyright, disclaimers and a contents list. It notes that the content draws on a March 2006 technical consultation in Montreux on sexual and reproductive health programmes and HPV vaccines and lists the participating experts. The acknowledgements name the UNFPA and WHO departments involved and say the note aims to alert stakeholders in several health programmes to key issues.
